To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cerebellar Purkinje cells and the target neurones of the deep cerebellar nuclei, are both affected by 3-acetyl-pyridine (3-AP) neurotoxicity.

1) the activity of the ECNs is permanently increased in 3-acetyl pyridine (3AP) treated rats and 2) the inhibitory control that PCs exert on the activity of the target ECNs is permanently lost in 3AP-treated rats.

the long lasting effects of 3-acetyl-pyridine-induced destruction of the inferior olive are a permanent impairment of Purkinje cells inhibitory control over the activity of their cerebellar target neurones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the cerebellum after a long lasting lesion of the climbing fibres.
the study of the effects of long-term deafferentation on the cerebellar cortical output.
a better understanding of the cerebellum functions and the mechanisms of recovery from cerebellar lesions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the long-term effects of the 3-AP-induced destruction of the inferior olive on the cerebellar circuitry are a reduction of the Purkinj cell inhibition of the cerebellum nuclear neurones.
the PC inhibition of the ECNs is permanently reduced in 3AP-treated rats, and the PC excitation of the same neurones is enhanced.
the cerebellum is a structure that is able to compensate the loss of afferents and, at the same time, to preserve the original function of the cerebellum, which is the coordination of movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
3-AP induces a long-lasting reduction of PC inhibition which is probably due to a loss of the PC-ECN synaptic connections.
the PCs, after a long lasting deafferentation, recover their excitability but not the inhibitory action exerted on their targets.
the long-term effects of IO destruction on the activity of the PCs and of their target cells in the ECNs is a reduction of the PC inhibition on the ECNs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PC inhibition of the ECNs is not only a transient phenomenon.
the cerebellar circuitry, which has been considered as a model of plasticity, is also characterized by a remarkable stability.
the long-term effects of cerebellar lesions on neuronal activity are not only due to a permanent loss of afferent inputs.
